what_it_does: Neural networks (AI models made of layers of multiplications) trained with many weights set to zero (called sparse models) should in theory be faster to run, because zero multiplications can be skipped. In practice, running a sparse model on a GPU (a chip optimized for dense parallel math) is often slower than running the dense version, because the special sparse number formats require extra bookkeeping — encoding which entries are non-zero, then decoding that map during computation — that costs more time than the skipped multiplications save. CROSS is a compiler (a tool that translates a model description into chip instructions) that analyzes where the zeros are clustered versus scattered, then automatically decides for each chunk of the model whether to use a sparse routine or a dense routine. A translation step rewrites the sparse parts of the computation graph into a form that dense, highly-tuned math libraries (called BLAS routines, which are the fastest known GPU matrix-multiplication implementations) can consume directly, so the dense path gets full GPU speed while the sparse path handles truly sparse regions.
